title: The Legacy of Rebbetzin Kanievsky: The Power of Prayer, Psalms and the Separation of Challah
source_file: מורשת הרבנית קנייבסקי_ כוח התפילה, התהילים והפרשת החלה.docx
content:
The Legacy of Rebbetzin Kanievsky: The Power of Prayer, Psalms and the Separation of Challah The Work, Torah Teaching and Public Leadership of Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky: A Historical, Social and Theological Analysis The text surveys the life and legacy of Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky, analyzing her growth out of the scholarly and spiritual elite of Lithuanian Jewry as the daughter of great Torah scholars. It details how she established an unprecedented model of female leadership that turned her home into a center of radical loving-kindness and spiritual counsel for thousands of women, combining stringent halakhic meticulousness with deep empathy. By presenting a practical theology of segulot that stresses the power of prayer and the refinement of character traits, the article explains her educational worldview and the importance of modesty in building the Jewish home. Finally, the source describes the processes by which her memory was institutionalized after her death and the continuity of her public work through her daughters, thereby establishing her standing as a key historical figure in shaping the world of women's Torah life. The Work, Torah Teaching and Public Leadership of Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky: A Historical, Social and Theological Analysis The Roots of Her Growth and the Intersection of the Scholarly and Spiritual Elites Rebbetzin Batsheva Esther Kanievsky (24 Shevat 5692, 1 February 1932 – 17 Tishrei 5772, 15 October 2011) is one of the most influential key figures in shaping the world of women's Torah life and in establishing a unique female spiritual leadership in the Haredi-Lithuanian public at the turn of the twenty-first century [cite: 1]. Her figure and leadership cannot be understood in isolation from her deep family roots, which represent the intersection of the two most prominent scholarly and spiritual elites in Lithuanian Jewry and in the Jerusalem of the Old Yishuv [cite: 1]. The Rebbetzin was born in the Meah Shearim neighborhood of Jerusalem, as the heir of glorious lines of lineage [cite: 1]. On her father's side, the halakhic decisor of the generation and the rabbi of the entire Diaspora, the Gaon Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, she imbibed the legacy of total diligence, stringent halakhic precision and uncompromising depth of study [cite: 1]. In her youth, alongside her practical work in bookkeeping, the Rebbetzin served as a close assistant to her father and helped him in the work of proofreading the writings of his grandfather, the renowned kabbalist of the period Rabbi Shlomo Elyashiv, author of the foundational kabbalistic work "Leshem Shevo ve-Achlamah" [cite: 1]. This early exposure to both the esoteric world and halakha instilled in her a reverent attitude toward the written word and toward halakhic texts [cite: 1]. On the side of her mother, Rebbetzin Sheina Chaya, Batsheva Esther was the beloved granddaughter of the Gaon and tzaddik Rabbi Aryeh Levin, known as "the father of the prisoners" [cite: 1]. In her childhood she used to accompany her grandfather on his frequent visits to the prisoners of the underground movements in the Mandate prisons, as well as on visits to the gravely ill and to the homes of lonely widows [cite: 1]. These encounters formed in her a worldview of radical loving-kindness, deep empathy for others and an ability to listen to wounded souls, qualities that later became the foundation of her public work [cite: 1]. On 7 Kislev 5712 she married the Gaon Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky, who was still studying in those days at the Lomza Yeshiva in Petach Tikva [cite: 1]. The match was proposed by Maran the Chazon Ish, who knew intimately the spiritual qualities of the bride and the scholarly greatness of the groom [cite: 1]. After their marriage the couple moved to live in the Chazon Ish neighborhood (Shikun Chazon Ish) in Bnei Brak [cite: 1]. There, out of extreme contentment with little and complete disregard for material things, the Rebbetzin built their shared home [cite: 2]. Her worldview rejected enjoyment of this world "even with a little finger," and was marked by constant joy in her lot [cite: 2]. It is told that in the first years of their marriage, when a certain sum of money unexpectedly came into her hands, she hastened to give it up for charity and for the most basic needs of the household, without leaving anything for personal luxuries [cite: 2]. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The Family Dynasty and the Continuity of the Generations The Kanievsky family produced a generation of Torah scholars and spiritual leaders, many of whom took an active part in preserving the Rebbetzin's legacy and in editing her writings [cite: 1, 3]. The following table presents the structure of the family dynasty and the role of the descendants in preserving the family memory: Name of the descendant Spouse Public role and preservation of the family legacy Rabbi Avraham Yeshayahu Kanievsky Among the heads of the institutions and of the Torah leadership in the Chazon Ish neighborhood in Bnei Brak [cite: 1]. Rabbi Shlomo Kanievsky Rosh yeshiva of the "Tiferet Tzion" yeshiva and rosh yeshiva of the "Kiryat Melech" yeshiva in Bnei Brak [cite: 1]. Rabbi Yitzchak Shaul Kanievsky A Torah scholar engaged in commemorating the legacy of his father and mother; he went over the writings of the book "Beit Imi" before its publication [cite: 1, 3]. Chana Steinman, of blessed memory (died 5774) The Gaon Rabbi Shraga Noach Steinman Wife of a rosh yeshiva; Rabbi Steinman was an active partner in proofreading and editing the writings in memory of his mother-in-law [cite: 1, 3]. Rebbetzin Leah Koldetsky The Gaon Rabbi Yitzchak Koldetsky Her mother's official successor in receiving women for blessing, counsel and salvation, at the explicit request of her father, Rabbi Chaim [cite: 1, 4]. Rebbetzin Ruth Tzvion The Gaon Rabbi Yehoshua Tzvion Author of the monumental biographical and educational book "Beit Imi," which documents the life, virtues and teaching of her mother [cite: 1, 3, 5]. Rebbetzin Bracha Braverman The Gaon Rabbi Zelig Braverman Wife of a rosh yeshiva, active in the education and spiritual guidance of the daughters of Israel [cite: 1]. Rebbetzin Dina Epstein The Gaon Rabbi Elazar David Epstein Active in disseminating Torah and in spiritual leadership in her community [cite: 1]. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The Model of Female Leadership in the Chazon Ish Neighborhood: Receiving the Public and the Institutional Structure From the 1990s onward a far-reaching social and spiritual transformation took place in the home of Rebbetzin Kanievsky, which challenged the traditional Lithuanian patterns of leadership [cite: 1]. The Rebbetzin began to receive women in her home for counsel, blessing and encouragement, a phenomenon that until then had been rare and almost nonexistent in the Lithuanian stream, which is characterized by a distinctly scholarly-male leadership [cite: 1]. The house at 23 Rashbam Street became a center of pilgrimage for thousands of women from all over the country and the world, who sought relief for their troubles [cite: 3, 5, 6]. Rebbetzin Kanievsky was described as "a one-woman institution" [cite: 6]. She was not content with giving verbal blessings, but established within her home an informal system of welfare and loving-kindness that included several active branches [cite: 6]: A soup kitchen: providing hot meals to needy women, families in distress and guests who came from afar [cite: 6]. A charity and free-loan fund: distributing money to the needy and to families that had fallen into debt [cite: 6]. A "clothing the naked" project: help in purchasing clothes and dowries for poor brides [cite: 6]. A system of aid to the sick and medical counseling: connecting patients with expert physicians and helping to obtain medications [cite: 6]. Her leadership was marked by infinite patience, especially toward people in hardship, the broken in spirit and troublesome individuals pushed to the margins of society [cite: 6]. Although she herself suffered many pains and ailments, she took care to hide them and never complained, so as not to sadden those who came through her doors [cite: 6]. The guiding motto of the home, which she passed on to her descendants and to those around her, was: "In my home no one is turned away" [cite: 6]. The Rebbetzin's daily reception of the public was conducted on a strict schedule: in the morning hours, between 10:30 and 13:00 (and on days of the Yom Kippur Katan prayer until 12:00), she received women individually [cite: 7]. Thursdays were devoted to sacred gatherings of mass separation of challah, which began at 17:00 [cite: 7, 8]. These events combined the baking of dough in the quantity requiring a blessing, moving stories of salvation, words of strengthening in faith and soul-stirring prayers [cite: 7, 8]. Many women used to bring to these gatherings notes with names for blessing, which at the end of the day were passed directly to her husband, Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky, for his perusal and blessing [cite: 7]. Despite her simplicity, the Rebbetzin managed a developed network of communication and took care to recite a special chapter of Psalms for each and every petitioner after she had left the room, out of a sense of genuine partnership in the other's sorrow [cite: 9]. She believed that "it is the Psalms that help!" and preferred the power of direct prayer over any other human mechanism [cite: 9]. The Rebbetzin also acted out of a protective approach toward the members of her extended family. A prominent example is her practice of concealing and playing down the wonders performed by her father-in-law (or, as she called him in the affectionate family term, "the Grandfather"), Maran Rabbi Yaakov Yisrael Kanievsky (the "Steipler") [cite: 10]. When supernatural events occurred in her presence, she hastened to warn her husband not to publicize them, out of concern that his becoming known as a wonder-worker would bring a flood of petitioners into his home and cause a severe neglect of Torah study, which she saw as a grave injury to the supreme value of Torah study [cite: 10]. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The Practical Theology of Segulah and Prayer The Torah thought of the Lithuanian stream is generally characterized by halakhic rationalism and by suspicion toward popular mysticism and segulot. However, Rebbetzin Kanievsky developed a unique practical theology that bridged this gap [cite: 5]. She succeeded in demystifying the concept of the "segulah," making clear to the women who turned to her that it is not a matter of independent "magic solutions" [cite: 5]. In her view, a segulah is a spiritual tool that can help only when it is accompanied by inner merits, the correction of character traits, spiritual resolutions and pure prayer from the heart [cite: 5]. To every request for help she used to answer: "If you want salvation, add a prayer to your prayers" [cite: 5]. The following table presents in concentrated form the main segulot that the Rebbetzin spread, their halakhic sources and the narratives accompanying them: The segulah / spiritual resolution The conceptual / halakhic source Area of effect Manner of practical application and the accompanying narrative The "Asher Yatzar" blessing read from the text and with intention The custom of Rabbi Chaim and the Rebbetzin [cite: 3, 5] General healing, and especially the resolution of problems in the digestive system [cite: 3, 5] Precise reading of the blessing from a wall chart or a decorated blessing card distributed in the thousands [cite: 3].
The narrative: a woman from abroad took it upon herself to recite the blessing in Hebrew from a prayer book for the sake of her father, who had undergone complex heart surgery; the blessing lasted about half an hour each time, and the father recovered completely against the doctors' forecasts [cite: 3]. Studying two laws of guarding one's speech (Shemirat ha-Lashon) every day A resolution of the Gaon Rabbi Yehuda Zev Segal of Manchester [cite: 5] Salvations in all matters: matches, fertility and healing [cite: 5] Consistent study of laws in the book "Chafetz Chaim" or "Netzor Leshonkha" [cite: 5].
The narrative: a woman who had been barren for seven years began daily study and was blessed with four children [cite: 5]; a girl who had been unconscious for two weeks, and immediately upon waking asked to know how many laws she had to make up because of her resolution to study every day [cite: 5]. Reciting "Nishmat Kol Chai" after the salvation The practice of Maran the Steipler in times of trouble and danger [cite: 5] A remedy for tangible situations of illness and danger [cite: 5] An advance undertaking, "without a vow," to recite the prayer after the rescue, and the distribution of booklets of the prayer [cite: 5].
The narrative: a child who smashed his leg in a fall from a height, and the doctors determined that he would not walk again without operations; under the Rebbetzin's guidance the "Nishmat" prayer was recited for every small improvement, and the child recovered completely without an operation [cite: 5]. Picturing the Tetragrammaton (the Name Havayah) and saying "There is none else besides Him" A resolution received from Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky [cite: 10] Removing fears and anxieties, especially before childbirth [cite: 10] Visual picturing of the holy letters in the air before the eyes and an oral declaration of the unity of God [cite: 10]. A natural preparation for the scalp A tradition of family home remedy [cite: 10] A remedy for severe hair loss [cite: 10] Mixing a spoonful of olive oil, a spoonful of castor oil, an egg yolk and drops of lemon juice; washing with the mixture for 20 minutes once a week after ordinary shampoo [cite: 10]. Reciting the "Yehi Ratzon" prayer before taking medicine Ruled as halakha in the Shulchan Arukh [cite: 3] Instilling the awareness that the Holy One, blessed be He, is the true healer [cite: 3] Reciting the formula: "May it be Your will that this undertaking be for me a complete healing, for You are a healer who heals freely" before every taking of a medicinal drug [cite: 3]. As an inseparable part of her educational teaching for the establishment of homes of Torah, the Rebbetzin guided mothers to direct their intention in a focused way at critical moments of prayer and of the blessings, so as to merit sons and grandsons who are Torah scholars and righteous [cite: 3]. She defined four main points of intention in the order of the daily and weekly prayers [cite: 3]: The blessing over the Torah: deep intention in the words "Ve-ha'arev na" (please make sweet) [cite: 3]. The blessing "Yotzer Or": special intention in the blessing "Ahavah Rabbah" for Torah study and its understanding [cite: 3]. The Kedushah order: intention in the request "that we may not labor in vain nor bring forth for confusion" in the passage "U-va le-Tzion" [cite: 3]. The prayers of the holy Sabbath: added intention in reciting the prayer "Yekum Purkan," which is intended for the success of those who study Torah [cite: 3]. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The Teaching of Modesty and the Construction of the Jewish Home In her personal conduct and in her encounters with the public, Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky presented a conservative and restrained position on everything concerning the laws of modesty and the appearance of the Jewish home, while closely guarding the walls of the Haredi-Lithuanian community, but with an empathetic and personal attitude toward each woman who turned to her [cite: 6, 11, 12]. On the question of covering the hair with a wig, the Rebbetzin supported the family ruling accepted in the house of the Chazon Ish and the house of the Steipler, according to which married women are permitted to wear a wig, and indeed the mother and wife of the Chazon Ish and the wife of the Steipler acted accordingly in practice [cite: 11]. At the same time, the Rebbetzin and her husband Rabbi Chaim firmly opposed the modern trends of long, loose wigs or ones made of natural hair that looks exactly like the woman's own hair, so that it is impossible to tell them apart [cite: 11]. Their halakhic position was that in cases where the wig looks exactly like natural hair and allows no visual distinction, one should be stringent and not wear it [cite: 11]. At the same time, she encouraged women who decided of their own accord to switch to covering their hair with a kerchief out of motives of holiness and personal spiritual awakening [cite: 13]. The Rebbetzin's opposition to commercial compromises in the realm of clothing highlighted her systemic conception of the boundaries of Haredi society [cite: 12]. When the question arose whether clothing stores in the Haredi sector were permitted to stock and sell clothes that were too colorful (such as pink or light purple) or skirts that did not reach the ankle, as a temporary solution for women who find it hard to keep full modesty, she answered with an absolute negative [cite: 12]. The Rebbetzin held that no legitimacy should be given to the sale of clothing that is not entirely kosher, even if the aim is to prevent those women from buying less modest clothes elsewhere, since the sanctity of the community takes precedence over any commercial compromise [cite: 12, 14]. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- The Institutionalization of Memory and the Transfer of the Authority of Leadership The sudden death of Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky at midday on the Sabbath of Chol ha-Moed Sukkot, 17 Tishrei 5772 (15 October 2011), as a result of a sudden cardiac event at her home in Bnei Brak, struck the Jewish world with deep shock [cite: 1, 15, 16]. In light of her death, the members of the family deliberated at length over whether to inform her aged father, the halakhic decisor of the generation Rabbi Elyashiv, of it, because of his fragile state of health and concern for his life [cite: 16]. Her massive funeral procession set out from her home toward the "Shomrei Shabbat" cemetery in Bnei Brak, where she was buried [cite: 1]. The process of institutionalizing the memory and commemoration of the Rebbetzin began immediately at the end of the shiv'ah [cite: 5]. Her daughter, Rebbetzin Ruth Tzvion, devoted herself to writing the monumental biographical book "Beit Imi" [cite: 3, 5, 17]. The book, which runs to 720 pages in its expanded edition, presents authentic testimonies from inside the home and is accompanied by dozens of rare original photographs [cite: 3, 5, 17]. The public importance of the book was further reinforced by the written approbation of her husband, Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky, who went over its pages carefully, confirmed their absolute accuracy and declared that "there is no greater book of mussar than this" [cite: 5]. The book became an instant bestseller in the Haredi sector and sold more than 5,000 copies in the first week of its distribution [cite: 5]. In order to prevent the interruption of the enterprise of loving-kindness and spiritual guidance that the Rebbetzin had established, a rapid process of transferring the authority of leadership took place [cite: 1, 4]. At the explicit request of Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky, her daughter, Rebbetzin Leah Koldetsky, took on the role of her successor and began to receive women for blessing and counsel in exactly the same format [cite: 1, 4]. The institutionalized reception of the public under the management of Rebbetzin Koldetsky became established in a fixed structure at 19 Rashbam Street (behind the women's section of the "Lederman" synagogue) [cite: 4]. Below are the details of the hours of reception and the arrangements of access for the general public today: Pregnant women and women before childbirth: received without an appointment for a blessing and an etrog on Sundays and Tuesdays at 12:00, and on Tuesdays and Wednesdays at 19:00 [cite: 4, 7]. Girls in their bat mitzvah year (bnot mitzvah): received on Sundays at 19:00 and on Mondays at 12:00 [cite: 4]. General reception of the public: held on Saturday nights (motza'ei Shabbat), Sundays, Mondays and Tuesdays from 21:00, by prior arrangement only, through a human operator [cite: 4]. Telephone appointment system: conducted at the number 052-7172233 on the designated days, in the evening hours between 21:00 and 21:10 (or until 21:30), to receive an appointment for the following day [cite: 4, 7]. This enterprise of continuity of female leadership, combining meticulous halakhic precision with supreme human sensitivity, ensures that the figure and teaching of Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky will continue to serve as a spiritual beacon and a source of inspiration for generations to come [cite: 1, 5]. -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- בת-שבע קניבסקי - The Work, Torah Teaching and Public Leadership of Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky: A Historical, Social and Theological Analysis
The text surveys the life and legacy of Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky, analyzing her growth out of the scholarly and spiritual elite of Lithuanian Jewry as the daughter of great Torah scholars. It details how she established an unprecedented model of female leadership that turned her home into a center of radical loving-kindness and spiritual counsel for thousands of women, combining stringent halakhic meticulousness with deep empathy. By presenting a practical theology of segulot that stresses the power of prayer and the refinement of character traits, the article explains her educational worldview and the importance of modesty in building the Jewish home. Finally, the source describes the processes by which her memory was institutionalized after her death and the continuity of her public work through her daughters, thereby establishing her standing as a key historical figure in shaping the world of women's Torah life.
The Work, Torah Teaching and Public Leadership of Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky: A Historical, Social and Theological Analysis
The Roots of Her Growth and the Intersection of the Scholarly and Spiritual Elites
Rebbetzin Batsheva Esther Kanievsky (24 Shevat 5692, 1 February 1932 – 17 Tishrei 5772, 15 October 2011) is one of the most influential key figures in shaping the world of women's Torah life and in establishing a unique female spiritual leadership in the Haredi-Lithuanian public at the turn of the twenty-first century [cite: 1]. Her figure and leadership cannot be understood in isolation from her deep family roots, which represent the intersection of the two most prominent scholarly and spiritual elites in Lithuanian Jewry and in the Jerusalem of the Old Yishuv [cite: 1].
The Rebbetzin was born in the Meah Shearim neighborhood of Jerusalem, as the heir of glorious lines of lineage [cite: 1]. On her father's side, the halakhic decisor of the generation and the rabbi of the entire Diaspora, the Gaon Rabbi Yosef Shalom Elyashiv, she imbibed the legacy of total diligence, stringent halakhic precision and uncompromising depth of study [cite: 1]. In her youth, alongside her practical work in bookkeeping, the Rebbetzin served as a close assistant to her father and helped him in the work of proofreading the writings of his grandfather, the renowned kabbalist of the period Rabbi Shlomo Elyashiv, author of the foundational kabbalistic work "Leshem Shevo ve-Achlamah" [cite: 1]. This early exposure to both the esoteric world and halakha instilled in her a reverent attitude toward the written word and toward halakhic texts [cite: 1].
On the side of her mother, Rebbetzin Sheina Chaya, Batsheva Esther was the beloved granddaughter of the Gaon and tzaddik Rabbi Aryeh Levin, known as "the father of the prisoners" [cite: 1]. In her childhood she used to accompany her grandfather on his frequent visits to the prisoners of the underground movements in the Mandate prisons, as well as on visits to the gravely ill and to the homes of lonely widows [cite: 1]. These encounters formed in her a worldview of radical loving-kindness, deep empathy for others and an ability to listen to wounded souls, qualities that later became the foundation of her public work [cite: 1].
On 7 Kislev 5712 she married the Gaon Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky, who was still studying in those days at the Lomza Yeshiva in Petach Tikva [cite: 1]. The match was proposed by Maran the Chazon Ish, who knew intimately the spiritual qualities of the bride and the scholarly greatness of the groom [cite: 1]. After their marriage the couple moved to live in the Chazon Ish neighborhood (Shikun Chazon Ish) in Bnei Brak [cite: 1]. There, out of extreme contentment with little and complete disregard for material things, the Rebbetzin built their shared home [cite: 2]. Her worldview rejected enjoyment of this world "even with a little finger," and was marked by constant joy in her lot [cite: 2]. It is told that in the first years of their marriage, when a certain sum of money unexpectedly came into her hands, she hastened to give it up for charity and for the most basic needs of the household, without leaving anything for personal luxuries [cite: 2].

The Model of Female Leadership in the Chazon Ish Neighborhood: Receiving the Public and the Institutional Structure
From the 1990s onward a far-reaching social and spiritual transformation took place in the home of Rebbetzin Kanievsky, which challenged the traditional Lithuanian patterns of leadership [cite: 1]. The Rebbetzin began to receive women in her home for counsel, blessing and encouragement, a phenomenon that until then had been rare and almost nonexistent in the Lithuanian stream, which is characterized by a distinctly scholarly-male leadership [cite: 1]. The house at 23 Rashbam Street became a center of pilgrimage for thousands of women from all over the country and the world, who sought relief for their troubles [cite: 3, 5, 6].
Rebbetzin Kanievsky was described as "a one-woman institution" [cite: 6]. She was not content with giving verbal blessings, but established within her home an informal system of welfare and loving-kindness that included several active branches [cite: 6]:
A soup kitchen: providing hot meals to needy women, families in distress and guests who came from afar [cite: 6].
A charity and free-loan fund: distributing money to the needy and to families that had fallen into debt [cite: 6].
A "clothing the naked" project: help in purchasing clothes and dowries for poor brides [cite: 6].
A system of aid to the sick and medical counseling: connecting patients with expert physicians and helping to obtain medications [cite: 6].
Her leadership was marked by infinite patience, especially toward people in hardship, the broken in spirit and troublesome individuals pushed to the margins of society [cite: 6]. Although she herself suffered many pains and ailments, she took care to hide them and never complained, so as not to sadden those who came through her doors [cite: 6]. The guiding motto of the home, which she passed on to her descendants and to those around her, was: "In my home no one is turned away" [cite: 6].
The Rebbetzin's daily reception of the public was conducted on a strict schedule: in the morning hours, between 10:30 and 13:00 (and on days of the Yom Kippur Katan prayer until 12:00), she received women individually [cite: 7]. Thursdays were devoted to sacred gatherings of mass separation of challah, which began at 17:00 [cite: 7, 8]. These events combined the baking of dough in the quantity requiring a blessing, moving stories of salvation, words of strengthening in faith and soul-stirring prayers [cite: 7, 8]. Many women used to bring to these gatherings notes with names for blessing, which at the end of the day were passed directly to her husband, Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky, for his perusal and blessing [cite: 7].
Despite her simplicity, the Rebbetzin managed a developed network of communication and took care to recite a special chapter of Psalms for each and every petitioner after she had left the room, out of a sense of genuine partnership in the other's sorrow [cite: 9]. She believed that "it is the Psalms that help!" and preferred the power of direct prayer over any other human mechanism [cite: 9].
The Rebbetzin also acted out of a protective approach toward the members of her extended family. A prominent example is her practice of concealing and playing down the wonders performed by her father-in-law (or, as she called him in the affectionate family term, "the Grandfather"), Maran Rabbi Yaakov Yisrael Kanievsky (the "Steipler") [cite: 10]. When supernatural events occurred in her presence, she hastened to warn her husband not to publicize them, out of concern that his becoming known as a wonder-worker would bring a flood of petitioners into his home and cause a severe neglect of Torah study, which she saw as a grave injury to the supreme value of Torah study [cite: 10].

The Practical Theology of Segulah and Prayer
The Torah thought of the Lithuanian stream is generally characterized by halakhic rationalism and by suspicion toward popular mysticism and segulot. However, Rebbetzin Kanievsky developed a unique practical theology that bridged this gap [cite: 5]. She succeeded in demystifying the concept of the "segulah," making clear to the women who turned to her that it is not a matter of independent "magic solutions" [cite: 5]. In her view, a segulah is a spiritual tool that can help only when it is accompanied by inner merits, the correction of character traits, spiritual resolutions and pure prayer from the heart [cite: 5]. To every request for help she used to answer: "If you want salvation, add a prayer to your prayers" [cite: 5].

She defined four main points of intention in the order of the daily and weekly prayers [cite: 3]:
The blessing over the Torah: deep intention in the words "Ve-ha'arev na" (please make sweet) [cite: 3].
The blessing "Yotzer Or": special intention in the blessing "Ahavah Rabbah" for Torah study and its understanding [cite: 3].
The Kedushah order: intention in the request "that we may not labor in vain nor bring forth for confusion" in the passage "U-va le-Tzion" [cite: 3].
The prayers of the holy Sabbath: added intention in reciting the prayer "Yekum Purkan," which is intended for the success of those who study Torah [cite: 3].

The Teaching of Modesty and the Construction of the Jewish Home
In her personal conduct and in her encounters with the public, Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky presented a conservative and restrained position on everything concerning the laws of modesty and the appearance of the Jewish home, while closely guarding the walls of the Haredi-Lithuanian community, but with an empathetic and personal attitude toward each woman who turned to her [cite: 6, 11, 12].
On the question of covering the hair with a wig, the Rebbetzin supported the family ruling accepted in the house of the Chazon Ish and the house of the Steipler, according to which married women are permitted to wear a wig, and indeed the mother and wife of the Chazon Ish and the wife of the Steipler acted accordingly in practice [cite: 11]. At the same time, the Rebbetzin and her husband Rabbi Chaim firmly opposed the modern trends of long, loose wigs or ones made of natural hair that looks exactly like the woman's own hair, so that it is impossible to tell them apart [cite: 11]. Their halakhic position was that in cases where the wig looks exactly like natural hair and allows no visual distinction, one should be stringent and not wear it [cite: 11]. At the same time, she encouraged women who decided of their own accord to switch to covering their hair with a kerchief out of motives of holiness and personal spiritual awakening [cite: 13].
The Rebbetzin's opposition to commercial compromises in the realm of clothing highlighted her systemic conception of the boundaries of Haredi society [cite: 12]. When the question arose whether clothing stores in the Haredi sector were permitted to stock and sell clothes that were too colorful (such as pink or light purple) or skirts that did not reach the ankle, as a temporary solution for women who find it hard to keep full modesty, she answered with an absolute negative [cite: 12]. The Rebbetzin held that no legitimacy should be given to the sale of clothing that is not entirely kosher, even if the aim is to prevent those women from buying less modest clothes elsewhere, since the sanctity of the community takes precedence over any commercial compromise [cite: 12, 14].

The Institutionalization of Memory and the Transfer of the Authority of Leadership
The sudden death of Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky at midday on the Sabbath of Chol ha-Moed Sukkot, 17 Tishrei 5772 (15 October 2011), as a result of a sudden cardiac event at her home in Bnei Brak, struck the Jewish world with deep shock [cite: 1, 15, 16]. In light of her death, the members of the family deliberated at length over whether to inform her aged father, the halakhic decisor of the generation Rabbi Elyashiv, of it, because of his fragile state of health and concern for his life [cite: 16]. Her massive funeral procession set out from her home toward the "Shomrei Shabbat" cemetery in Bnei Brak, where she was buried [cite: 1].
The process of institutionalizing the memory and commemoration of the Rebbetzin began immediately at the end of the shiv'ah [cite: 5]. Her daughter, Rebbetzin Ruth Tzvion, devoted herself to writing the monumental biographical book "Beit Imi" [cite: 3, 5, 17]. The book, which runs to 720 pages in its expanded edition, presents authentic testimonies from inside the home and is accompanied by dozens of rare original photographs [cite: 3, 5, 17]. The public importance of the book was further reinforced by the written approbation of her husband, Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky, who went over its pages carefully, confirmed their absolute accuracy and declared that "there is no greater book of mussar than this" [cite: 5]. The book became an instant bestseller in the Haredi sector and sold more than 5,000 copies in the first week of its distribution [cite: 5].
In order to prevent the interruption of the enterprise of loving-kindness and spiritual guidance that the Rebbetzin had established, a rapid process of transferring the authority of leadership took place [cite: 1, 4]. At the explicit request of Rabbi Chaim Kanievsky, her daughter, Rebbetzin Leah Koldetsky, took on the role of her successor and began to receive women for blessing and counsel in exactly the same format [cite: 1, 4].
The institutionalized reception of the public under the management of Rebbetzin Koldetsky became established in a fixed structure at 19 Rashbam Street (behind the women's section of the "Lederman" synagogue) [cite: 4]. Below are the details of the hours of reception and the arrangements of access for the general public today:
Pregnant women and women before childbirth: received without an appointment for a blessing and an etrog on Sundays and Tuesdays at 12:00, and on Tuesdays and Wednesdays at 19:00 [cite: 4, 7].
Girls in their bat mitzvah year (bnot mitzvah): received on Sundays at 19:00 and on Mondays at 12:00 [cite: 4].
General reception of the public: held on Saturday nights (motza'ei Shabbat), Sundays, Mondays and Tuesdays from 21:00, by prior arrangement only, through a human operator [cite: 4].
Telephone appointment system: conducted at the number 052-7172233 on the designated days, in the evening hours between 21:00 and 21:10 (or until 21:30), to receive an appointment for the following day [cite: 4, 7].
This enterprise of continuity of female leadership, combining meticulous halakhic precision with supreme human sensitivity, ensures that the figure and teaching of Rebbetzin Batsheva Kanievsky will continue to serve as a spiritual beacon and a source of inspiration for generations to come [cite: 1, 5].
